title: Embedded Figures
summary: Find a small figure hidden inside a bigger one exactly as drawn — same size and orientation (rotation is not allowed). Anchor on the most distinctive stroke, usually a slant, and reject options that are flips or rotations of the true part.

subtopics.title: Finding the hidden part in a figure
subtopics.concept:
A complex figure is given and you must find which option figure is **hidden inside it exactly as drawn** — same size, same angles, same orientation. The standard SSC instruction is *rotation is not allowed*.

Method:
1. In each option, pick its most unusual stroke — a lone slanting line, an odd-length side, a T-junction.
2. Search the main figure for that stroke in the **same direction**.
3. Trace the rest of the option from there; every line must be present in the main figure (it may be part of a longer line).

Distractors are usually the correct part flipped, rotated or with one line changed. That is why orientation matters more than the general shape.

tricks.title: Anchor on the slant
tricks.body: A slanting line has only two possible directions (/ or \). Check whether the main figure even has the option's slant in the right place; this rejects mirror-image distractors in seconds.

example.q: **Q.** The main figure has only \ diagonals. An option contains a / slant. Can it be embedded?
example.solution: No — without a / line anywhere in the main figure that option is impossible.

mistakes: Accepting a part that fits only after rotating or flipping it.
Ignoring length: a line in the option that is longer than any matching line in the figure cannot fit.
Forgetting that a short option line may be a piece of a longer line in the figure.

subtopics.title: Which figure contains the given part
subtopics.concept:
The reverse form: one small figure is given and each option is a bigger figure. Choose the option in which the small figure appears **as it is**.

Scan each option for the part's key stroke, then confirm the rest. Options that nearly contain it usually lack one line or have it running the other way.

tricks.title: Eliminate by the missing line
tricks.body: Count the part's line directions (horizontal, vertical, /, \). Any option missing one of these directions is out immediately.

example.q: **Q.** The part has a horizontal, a vertical and a \ line. Option B has no \ line at all. Keep B?

mistakes: Choosing an option where the part fits only after rotation.
Stopping at the first partial match without checking every line.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Hidden part in square grid figure
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Square with diagonals/midlines; options are small line clusters.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor on the slant direction, then trace; reject flips and rotations.
Match lengths as well as directions.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One small figure in the question, bigger figures in the options.
pyqPatterns.approach: Eliminate options lacking one of the part's line directions.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options are rotations/flips of the same shape.
pyqPatterns.approach: Only the orientation that matches the figure is correct.

solvedExamples.q: In which option is the figure given in the question **embedded** as a part (rotation is not allowed)?
solvedExamples.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 34 22" width="34" height="22" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="5" y1="5" x2="17" y2="17"/><line x1="17" y1="5" x2="17" y2="17"/><line x1="17" y1="17" x2="29" y2="17"/></svg>
solvedExamples.solution: The part is a \ slant whose lower end meets a vertical line coming down and a horizontal line going off to the right. In the first figure this happens at the bottom: the lower half of the long diagonal ends where the vertical line meets the bottom edge, and the bottom edge supplies the horizontal line. The second figure has only a / slant; the third has no vertical line at the lower end of its slant; in the fourth the horizontal line at the slant's lower end runs to the left, not the right.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Look for the part's most unusual stroke first; reject options where it is missing or runs the wrong way.

practice.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 34 34" width="34" height="34" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="5" y1="17" x2="17" y2="5"/><line x1="17" y1="5" x2="17" y2="17"/><line x1="17" y1="5" x2="29" y2="5"/><line x1="17" y1="17" x2="17" y2="29"/></svg>
practice.solution: The part is a / slant rising to a point, a horizontal line going right from that point and a vertical line going down from it. Only the first figure has the / slant cutting the top-left corner exactly where the vertical line meets the top edge; the top edge supplies the horizontal line. The second has the slant the other way; in the third no vertical line goes down from the upper end of the slant; in the fourth the slant is at the bottom.
practice.shortcut: Look for the part's most unusual stroke first; reject options where it is missing or runs the wrong way.
